steps.title: 1. Orient and prepare the container
steps.goal: Map a substantial repository and distinguish upstream code from the course examples.
steps.opening: Rich formats terminal output. You do not need to understand every module to follow one useful behaviour.
steps.task: Read READING.md and scan Explorer for rich/, tests/, examples/, docs/ and reading/. Use Quick Open for pyproject.toml to identify dependencies. Run setup once in the course container; it downloads pinned dependencies. Write a short directory map.
steps.expected: Setup reports Rich loading from this project source tree. reading/ contains separate course helpers; rich/ and tests/ are upstream.
steps.hint: Look for a library package, examples that call it, and tests that assert its behaviour. Defer benchmarks, release tools and unrelated features.
steps.reflection: Which directory would you open to answer a question about a public API, and why?

nextAction.task: Locate only rich/ and reading/. Note which contains upstream library code and which contains the course callers.

steps.title: 2. Start from a tiny caller
steps.goal: Choose one concrete input and predict its output before entering library internals.
steps.opening: A small caller gives a large repository a focused reading route. Begin with plain_text in the course examples.
steps.task: Open reading/examples.py at plain_text. Identify the Console options, StringIO output and print call. Predict repr(output.getvalue()), including the newline. Run the example. Record the observed value and one question about how it was produced.
steps.expected: The example prints the representation of Hello, reader! followed by a newline. This is an observed output, not a test of understanding.
steps.hint: StringIO captures output in memory. The outer built-in print displays repr; the inner console.print is the library call you will trace.
steps.reflection: Why capture output instead of relying on terminal colors for this first investigation?

nextAction.task: Read only plain_text. Write the string passed to console.print and predict whether the captured value ends with a newline.

steps.title: 3. Navigate into Console.print
steps.goal: Find a method in a long file and identify its major calls without reading the entire file.
steps.opening: Large files are navigable through symbols and questions. Focus on where arguments become renderable objects.
steps.task: From the caller, use Go to Definition if available. Otherwise Quick Open rich/console.py and search def print(. Coach's file link jumps there. Skim the signature and find _collect_renderables, render and buffer extension. Trace those calls for the plain string input.
steps.expected: The same output is reproduced. Your notes identify the public method and the next internal boundary, without treating every branch as executed.
steps.hint: Use Go to Symbol in Editor or exact text search in console.py. Find the path for your actual arguments; leave JSON, logging and SVG export for another question.
steps.reflection: Which branch is irrelevant to this input, and how can you tell?

nextAction.task: Within Console.print, find the call to _collect_renderables. Name one argument passed in and the variable receiving its result. Stop at that boundary.

steps.title: 4. Trace string to Text
steps.goal: Follow a change in representation across methods and modules.
steps.opening: The printed string is not the final representation. Console prepares renderable objects before converting them to terminal segments.
steps.task: Find _collect_renderables and its call to render_str. Follow the no-markup route into Text construction. Record input type, output type and who owns the conversion. Use workspace search for callers when symbol navigation is unavailable.
steps.expected: Your trace links the caller's string to Text and distinguishes preparation from final output.
steps.hint: Place the cursor near render_str before asking Coach about it; the shared context will show that region. Trace only the markup=False route first.
steps.reflection: What would change in the route if markup were enabled?

nextAction.task: Inside _collect_renderables, find the string branch and its render_str call. Follow the markup=False route and name the returned type.

steps.title: 5. Read a transformation
steps.goal: Separate plain content from style metadata and connect a parser to its tests.
steps.opening: Markup makes the representation visible: tags become style spans while the plain text loses the tags.
steps.task: Read the markup example, then Text.from_markup and markup.render. Predict text.plain, span boundaries and uncolored captured output. Run it. Read test_from_markup to locate its exact assertion; identify parsing separately from rendering.
steps.expected: Plain text has no tags; the bold span covers Hello; captured output has no terminal color escapes.
steps.hint: Track two values: text characters and spans. A style can exist in the Text object even when the output device does not emit colors.
steps.reflection: Which observation supports the claim that parsing and terminal color output are separate?

nextAction.task: Read the markup example and write two predictions: the plain characters and the range covered by bold. Compare each separately with the output.

steps.title: 6. Follow the rendering protocol
steps.goal: Explain how different objects participate in rendering without a separate print method for each type.
steps.opening: Python protocols can be ordinary methods rather than a shared base class. Trace one custom renderable to understand the contract.
steps.task: Read Greeting.__rich_console__ in the example. Follow Console.render, rich.protocol.rich_cast, Text.__rich_console__ and Segment. Predict the yielded object and final output, then run protocol. Distinguish yielding a Text object from writing bytes to the terminal.
steps.expected: The custom greeting renders successfully. Your explanation names the protocol method and the recursive conversion to segments.
steps.hint: In Console.render, find how __rich_console__ is obtained, then what happens to each item it yields. Compare a Segment with another renderable.
steps.reflection: Why can Greeting work without inheriting from Console or Text?

nextAction.task: Read only Greeting.__rich_console__. Identify the type of the yielded object, then locate where Console.render handles that type.

steps.title: 7. Read upstream tests as evidence
steps.goal: Use tests to recover a contract and recognize the limits of a selected test run.
steps.opening: Tests expose concrete input/output claims. Read their setup and assertions before running them.
steps.task: Use Quick Open for tests/test_console.py and find test_print, test_print_multiple and test_print_empty. Predict each captured value, then run the focused tests. Explain which Console behaviour each assertion covers and what remains outside these three tests.
steps.expected: Three selected upstream tests pass. This does not mean the entire upstream suite has run or prove your understanding.
steps.hint: StringIO and fixed Console options make assertions repeatable. Read the expected string literally, including spaces and newlines.
steps.reflection: Which boundary case would you investigate next, and which existing test might cover it?

nextAction.task: Read only test_print. Write its input and exact expected string, including whitespace, before running the selected tests.

steps.title: 8. Trace a feature across modules
steps.goal: Build a focused call/data map for a table using the same navigation method.
steps.opening: Transfer the method to a richer object. A table stores rows, measures columns and yields renderable output.
steps.task: Read the table example. Follow Table.add_row, Table.__rich_console__ and _render. Look into measure.py only when the trace needs column widths. Predict the rows and column alignment, then run table. Draw a path from caller to row storage to measurement to rendering.
steps.expected: A two-column book table appears. Your trace separates stored cell content, width calculation and generated output.
steps.hint: Search for add_row to find the mutation, then __rich_console__ to find the rendering entry. Follow one width calculation before expanding the whole call graph.
steps.reflection: Where would you investigate a wrong column width versus a missing row?

nextAction.task: Choose one add_row call. List its cell values, then follow where Table stores those values before looking at width calculation.

steps.title: 9. Compare a boundary and its tests
steps.goal: Distinguish a behaviour claim from a hypothesis and support it with upstream assertions.
steps.opening: Use a contrast to sharpen your model: ordinary rows versus no columns, valid renderables versus invalid values.
steps.task: Read test_no_columns and test_not_renderable in tests/test_table.py. Find the branches they exercise in table.py, predict the outcomes, then run the table tests. Record the supporting assertion and one path you have not verified.
steps.expected: The focused table test file runs. Notes explain specific tested boundaries rather than declaring the whole library correct.
steps.hint: Follow the pytest.raises block as a statement about one error condition. Compare it with the single newline asserted for a table with no columns.
steps.reflection: What source evidence links each test to the branch you identified?

nextAction.task: Read only test_not_renderable. Identify the rejected input and expected exception, then find the matching check in Table.add_row.

steps.title: 10. Make your own reading route
steps.goal: Apply the navigation method to a nearby behaviour and explain the evidence and assistance behind your conclusions.
steps.opening: Choose a question that fits the files you now know, such as escaped markup or printing multiple Text objects.
steps.task: Select one new case in tests/test_markup.py. Record the question, prediction, path/symbol trace and assertion before running the markup tests. Finish READING_NOTES.md with remaining uncertainties and assistance. Save a local checkpoint if useful; explore other Rich features in the full repository when ready.
steps.expected: Markup tests run and your notes make the investigation reproducible. Coach help and a local checkpoint are not independent mastery or an official submission.
steps.hint: Search a literal input from a test, follow only the parser branch it triggers, and explain why its assertion follows. Ask Coach for one smaller step if the trace becomes too broad.
steps.reflection: How would you begin the next unfamiliar repository using what worked here?

nextAction.task: Choose test_render_escape. Copy one literal input and its expected plain text into your notes, then locate the parser branch that explains it.
